newsitem.title: UK: UK shares hope no-risks budget may lift rate gloom.
newsitem.headline: UK shares hope no-risks budget may lift rate gloom.

text.p: A gentle squeeze on the brakes of the British economy in Chancellor Kenneth Clarke's budget next week would be the best possible news for a London stock market jittery over rising interest rates, market watchers said.
Next week's budget provides a key test of economic policy in the dying months of the current Conservative party administration, which must call an election by May next year.
Yet for the stock market, the best budget would be a cautious package which passes up the chance for tax cuts which could stoke growth and further add to inflation risks.
"What the market wants is prudence above and beyond all else," said Andy Hartwill, equity strategist at brokerage SocGen.

Prospects of higher rates have already propelled the pound sharply higher as international investment funds flood into the currency seeking the higher short-term return on sterling bonds and cash deposits.
Yet a surging pound is putting a double squeeze on shares -- making British exports less competitive and eroding the sterling value of the profits companies make overseas.
If Clarke's budget adds fuel to the fire, the markets would quickly conclude that rates will be jacked up still higher in coming months to dampen growth and ward off inflation.
Specific budget measures could of course be significant for individual stocks and sectors.

Last year for instance, Clarke gave brewers and distillers a boost by cutting whisky duties and leaving duties on wine and beer unchanged, in response to lobbying from the industry over surging imports from France where duties are lower.

And the market could be unsettled by further measures to reduce the tax credit for pension funds on dividend payments -- making equity investments less attractive to some of the biggest investors in the market.
There is also a slim chance of extra tax-raising measures such as a windfall tax on utilities.
Yet it will be Clarke's overall economic stance that will determine the market's reaction.

"The looser the Budget is, the greater the danger that they will have to tighten on the monetary side and the stronger the currency will be," said Corey Miller, strategist at Credit Lyonnais Laing. "All that will be bad for the equity market."

"The best thing for the economy would actually be to raise taxes to take the emphasis away from monetary policy," Miller said. "If he plays things safe then hopefully that will take as much of the pressure off raising interest rates as possible."
Some said the market was already looking ahead to the budget in expectation of a benign package.
"It is increasingly evident that the Chancellor is unlikely to give away much on the tax front," said Michael Beggs, fund manager at investment group Guinness Flight.

"Clearly he doesn't have many options anyway, the markets would be unforgiving and he would have to drive up rates even higher." Despite hitting a record high in October, the UK's blue chip FTSE 100 index has underperformed other leading markets recently amid worries about rising interest rates and the strong pound.
Strategists said tax cuts of between two and three billion pounds -- including a cut of perhaps one percent in income tax, but offset by spending cuts elsewhere -- were probably discounted.

Yet the burning issue for the equity market is the likely trend of interest rates next year and the level of sterling -- as well as the fact that this year's budget could anyway be superceded by an incoming Labour administration in 1997.

"If he delivers a prudent budget, I think bond markets would like it and that would help equities," said Miller at Laing. "But people are looking ahead to a Labour budget a few weeks after the election so it is not straightforward this time."
